```{r}
# Part 1: Exponential Distribution

# Load dataset into code
data <- read.csv("data.csv")
idling_time <- data[, 2]
# Calculate core parameters
exponential_mean <- mean(idling_time)
cat("Exponential Mean: ", exponential_mean)

lambda <- 1 / exponential_mean
cat("Lambda: ", lambda)

# PDF parameters on peak spikes and volatility at x = 2
x <- 2
pdf_at_2 <- dexp(x, rate = lambda)
cat("PDF at x = 2: ", pdf_at_2)

pdf_mean <- dexp(exponential_mean, rate = lambda)
cat("PDF at mean: ", pdf_mean)

pdf <- pdf_at_2 / pdf_mean
cat("Congestion factor at peak traffic: ", pdf)


# PDF Analysis: Evaluating the Probability Density Function (PDF) at x = 2 to simulate a scenario where students come in more frequent and bigger batches as opposed to the experiment's spry 8 second arrival rate. When the yielded PDF value of 0.09790 is compared to set mean of 0.04631, the likelihood of a 2 second arrival interval becomes 2.1 times more likely to happen. This provides well-documented proof of "pack behavior" on campus: students do not and rarely pass throughsecurity checks in a homogenized, evenly-spaced stream. Instead, traffic travels in dense, rapid-fire clusters especially during peak hours. When these peak spikes hit, the guards are subjected to a wave of back-to-back arrivals that carries twice the baseline gate arrivals of usual campus traffic.


# CDF parameters on line congestion and line accumulation during peak hours 
y <- 2
cdf <- pexp(x, rate = lambda)
cat("Probability of line congestion at peak hours: ", cdf)

line_congestion_per_second <- 1 / 2
cat("Number of students arriving at security gate per second: ", line_congestion_per_second)

line_congestion <- line_congestion_per_second * 60
cat("Number of students arriving at security gate per minute: ", line_congestion)

# CDF Analysis: Using the Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) to isolate the exact threshold where the security check start to congest during peak arrival hours, we find a 22.27% probability that consecutive student arrivals occur within 2 seconds or less. Because each security guard takes an average of 4 seconds to inspect a bag, the security checks operate at its absolute maximum capacity threshold at precisely 2 seconds. Therefore, this CDF metric proves that nearly one-quarter (22.27%) of all incoming student traffic arrives at a rate that saturate the security check gates at certain hours of the day leaving the system vulnerable to immediate queue building at a rate of 0.50 students per second lost.



# Findings: 

# Scenario: Campus Security Gate Foot Traffic at main perimeter entrance. This study models student arrival gaps using an Exponential Distribution to evaluate how effectively a two-guard team handles real-world student arrivals.

# Data Collection Process: Ground observations were simulated and recorded tracking 50 consecutive student entries during a standard mid-morning window (9:00 AM – 10:30 AM). Using a stopwatch split-timer, the researcher logged the exact time gap (in seconds) between consecutive student arrivals at the security gate face. Total elapsed tracking time was 397 seconds.

# Computed Parameters:
	# Sample Size: 50 students
	# Sample Mean: 7.94 seconds between arrivals
	# Rate Parameter: 0.12594 arrivals per second

# Interpretations and Real-World Implications: 
    # PDF Analysis: Evaluating the PDF reveals that a rapid-fire 2-second arrival gap during peak hours has a density of 0.09790, making it 2.115 times more likely to happen than an arrival at the 7.94-second mean. This mathematically proves campus "pack behavior" (students clump in groups).

    # CDF Analysis: The CDF shows a 22.27% probability that students arrive within 2 seconds or less. Because two guards can process a maximum combined capacity of 1 student every 2 seconds, nearly one-quarter of all traffic saturates the gate during peak hours.

    # Queue Spillover: At this 2-second saturation point, any gate complication or second lost causes the line to immediately compound at a net rate of 0.50 students per second, adding 1 student every 2 seconds. A minor 30-second stall could generate 15 students onto the line.


# Graphing
# Create base density histogram using raw data
hist(idling_time, prob = TRUE, breaks = 12,
     main = "Observed Gaps vs. Fitted Exponential Curve",
     xlab = "Arrival Gaps (Seconds)", ylab = "Probability Density",
     col = "lightgray", border = "darkgray", xlim = c(0,30), ylim = c(0, 0.14))

# Generate points for exponential curve
x_seq <- seq(0, 30, by = 0.1)
y_curve <- dexp(x_seq, rate = lambda)
lines(x_seq, y_curve, col = "blue", lwd = 2.5)

# Shade PDF from 0 to 2 seconds
x_shade <- seq(0, 2, by = 0.01)
y_shade <- dexp(x_shade, rate = lambda)
polygon(c(0, x_shade, 2), c(0, y_shade, 0),
        col = rgb(1, 0, 0, alpha = 0.3), border = NA)

# Add legend and annotations
abline(v = exponential_mean, col = "darkgreen", lty = 2, lwd = 1.5)
points(2, dexp(2, rate = lambda), col = "red", pch = 19, cex = 1.5)
legend("topright", 
       legend = c("Observed Data", "Exponential PDF", "System Mean", "0-2s Overload Zone"),
       col = c("lightgray", "blue", "darkgreen", rgb(1, 0, 0, alpha = 0.3)), 
       lty = c(1, 1, 2, NA), 
       lwd = c(8, 2.5, 1.5, NA), 
       pch = c(NA, NA, NA, 15), 
       pt.cex = c(1, 1, 1, 2))
text(2.5, dexp(2, rate = lambda) + 0.01, labels = "x = 2s Limit", col = "darkred", font = 2)
text(exponential_mean + 2.5, 0.12, labels = paste("Mean =", round(exponential_mean, 2), "s"), col = "darkgreen")
```

```{r}
# Part 2: Normal Distributions

# Load data into code
data_2 <- read.csv("data.csv")
inspection_time <- data_2[, 3]

# Calculate core parameters
normal_mean <- mean(inspection_time)
stdev <- sd(inspection_time)

# Construct frequency distribution table
inspection_table <- data.frame(
  "Inspection Duration" = c(3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10),
  "Frequency" = c(7, 12, 3, 10, 6, 5, 5, 2),
  check.names = FALSE
)

total_n <- sum(inspection_table[["Frequency"]])

inspection_table[["Relative Frequency"]] <- inspection_table[["Frequency"]] / total_n
inspection_table[["Cumulative Frequency"]] <- cumsum(inspection_table[["Frequency"]])
inspection_table[["Cumulative Relative Frequency"]] <- cumsum(inspection_table[["Relative Frequency"]])

knitr::kable(inspection_table, format = "markdown")

# Create normal distribution curve
duration  <- c(3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10)
frequency <- c(7, 12, 3, 10, 6, 5, 5, 2)
raw_data  <- rep(duration, times = frequency)
total_n   <- sum(frequency)
bin_width <- 1
x_values <- seq(min(duration) - 1, max(duration) + 1, length.out = 200)
y_counts <- dnorm(x_values, mean = normal_mean, sd = stdev) * total_n * bin_width
plot(
  x_values, y_counts, 
  type = "l", 
  lwd = 3, 
  col = "darkblue",
  main = "Frequency vs Inspection Duration",
  xlab = "Inspection Duration", 
  ylab = "Frequency",
  ylim = c(0, max(frequency) + 2), 
  las = 1
)

# Percent data within 1, 2, and 3 standard deviations from the mean
pct_stdev <- sum(raw_data >= (normal_mean - 1 * stdev) & raw_data <= (normal_mean + 1 * stdev)) / total_n * 100
cat("Percent data within 1 standard deviation: ", pct_stdev)

pct_stdev_2 <- sum(raw_data >= (normal_mean - 2 * stdev) & raw_data <= (normal_mean + 2 * stdev)) / total_n * 100
cat("Percent data within 2 standard deviation: ", pct_stdev_2)

pct_stdev_3 <- sum(raw_data >= (normal_mean - 3 * stdev) & raw_data <= (normal_mean + 3 * stdev)) / total_n * 100
cat("Percent data within 3 standard deviation: ", pct_stdev_3)


# Findings: Security checks follow a normal distribution centered at an average (μ) of 5.82 seconds. While the Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) shows 64% of students clear quickly in 6 seconds or less (with 38% taking 4 seconds or less), a heavy right tail isolates a 36% risk zone where bag complications delay inspections to 7–10 seconds. Because the two-guard gate has a combined average capacity of one student every 2.91 seconds, when peak hours hit the gates it runs an operational deficit against students arriving at said gates. When a guard gets trapped in the 10-second slow zone, the gate degrades to a single lane and capacity is halved. Facing 2-second arrival bursts at this reduced speed forces a net queue growth of 0.50 students per second, meaning a single 10-second stall cause a 5 student long line. 
```
